explanations.explanation: The man says, “Lord, have mercy on my son…” so his begging is for his boy. He gets down on his knees and asks for mercy, and nothing in his words is for himself. I think a dad who kneels in front of a crowd has already stopped caring who's watching. Then he tells Jesus what his son is going through.

Fair guess, friend, but the man says, “Lord, have mercy on my son…” This passage never mentions a daughter. The one he's begging for is his boy. He kneels, asks for mercy, and then lays out the seizures.
No servant shows up anywhere in this scene. The man says, “Lord, have mercy on my son…” and then describes what the boy is suffering. I think his whole heart is with his child.

The man says the opposite. He tells Jesus, “I brought him to Your disciples, but they could not heal him.” So the man says the disciples could not heal his son. He is kneeling in front of Jesus when he says it.

That's right. The man tells Jesus, “I brought him to Your disciples, but they could not heal him.” So he brought his son to the disciples first, and they could not heal him. Now he is the one kneeling in front of Jesus.

Jesus says, “Bring the boy here to Me.” After the strong words, the next thing out of His mouth is a way forward for the boy. He doesn't send the dad off or tell him to come back later. He asks for the boy to be brought right to Him.

Jesus doesn't point the dad toward a priest or anyone else. He says, “Bring the boy here to Me.” Right after His strong words, the boy is what He turns to. I think that tells us those words weren't the end of the story for that boy.

No waiting is mentioned in this passage. Jesus says, “Bring the boy here to Me.” Then Jesus rebuked the demon, and the boy was healed from that moment (Matthew 17:18). Nothing gets put off until tomorrow.
The text says, “Then Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of the boy…” The demon is what Jesus speaks to, and it leaves. The boy was healed from that moment. A rebuke from Jesus is all it took.
Not a fever this time, friend. The text says Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of the boy. That's what He speaks to in this scene. The boy was healed from that moment.

Jesus did rebuke the winds and the sea in another story (Matthew 8:26), so I see where that came from. In this scene, though, the text says He rebuked the demon, and it came out of the boy. Different story, same Jesus speaking with authority. This boy was healed from that moment.
The text says the boy was healed from that moment. There is no mention of days of slowly getting better. Jesus rebuked the demon, it came out, and the healing was done. Nothing here is slow.
Right, friend. After Jesus rebuked the demon, it came out of the boy, and “…he was healed from that moment.” There are no days of waiting and no slow recovery in the text. It happens at once.

explanations.answer: Why couldn’t we drive it out
explanations.explanation: The disciples ask, “Why couldn’t we drive it out?” They came to Jesus privately to ask it. They had tried to heal the boy and could not. I think they had a hard question on their minds, and they took it to the right person.

Nobody asks that here, friend. The disciples come to Jesus privately and ask, “Why couldn’t we drive it out?” I think that sounds like people looking at themselves, not questioning Jesus. Jesus answers them with, “Because you have so little faith…”
Nobody asks that here, friend. The disciples come to Jesus privately and ask, “Why couldn’t we drive it out?” Their question is about the boy and the demon. It's not about Jesus going anywhere.
Jesus answers, “Because you have so little faith…” That's the reason He gives, and I'm not adding one of my own. Then He goes right into talking about a mustard seed. Faith is the whole topic here.
Strength sounds like it could fit, but it's not what Jesus says. He answers, “Because you have so little faith…” The reason He gives is faith, plain and simple. Muscles never come up in this answer.

Jesus doesn't say they needed more practice. He says, “Because you have so little faith…” I can see why it's a tempting pick, because practice fixes a lot of things in a kitchen. Here, the reason Jesus gives is faith.

Jesus says, “…if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move.” He talks about faith by its size, and He picks a seed. Then He adds, “Nothing will be impossible for you.” Every word of that is what He says.

Sand sounds like a good guess, but Jesus doesn't use it. He says, “…if you have faith the size of a mustard seed…” That seed-sized faith is the kind He says can speak to a mountain: “…you can say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move.” Sand never comes up.

Jesus doesn't bring up water here. He says, “…if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move.” His comparison is a seed. A drop of water never enters the conversation.

Jesus says, “Nothing will be impossible for you.” He says it right after talking about faith the size of a mustard seed. Those are His exact words to His disciples, and they come with the mountain moving from here to there. It's the last thing He says in this part.

The text says the opposite. After talking about faith the size of a mustard seed, Jesus tells the disciples, “Nothing will be impossible for you.” Those are His words, and they come right after the mountain moving from here to there.

Jesus says, “They will kill Him…” This is a heavy one, and I think it was hard for the disciples to hear. He is saying it about Himself, since the Son of Man is the name He uses for Himself (Mark 2:10).
That's not what Jesus says, friend. He says, “They will kill Him…” It's a heavy line, and I won't dress it up. Nothing in these words is about a crown.

Jesus doesn't say they will send Him away. He says, “They will kill Him, and on the third day He will be raised to life.” It's a heavy thing to hear, so I'll just say it plainly. He's the one speaking about Himself, since the Son of Man is the name He uses for Himself (Mark 2:10).

Jesus says, “…on the third day He will be raised to life.” He says it right after telling them He will be killed. So the heavy news and the promise are in the same breath. Those are His words, and they stand together.

The text says otherwise. Jesus says, “They will kill Him, and on the third day He will be raised to life.” The raising to life is part of what He tells them. It's in the very same sentence as the heavy part.

The text says, “And the disciples were deeply grieved.” Jesus had just told them He would be killed. I think anybody would be grieved to hear that about someone they follow. It's sad news, and the text doesn't hide that.
The text doesn't say amazed. It says, “And the disciples were deeply grieved.” They had just heard that Jesus would be killed. Grief is what the passage gives us.
Glad isn't the word the text uses. It says, “And the disciples were deeply grieved.” After hearing Jesus say they will kill Him, I think that makes sense. This part of the passage is a sad one.

explanations.answer: Whether Jesus pays the two drachmas
explanations.explanation: The collectors ask Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, “Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas?” They bring the question to Peter, but it's about his Teacher. Peter is the one who gets asked. Jesus is the one the question is about.

explanations.answer: Whether Peter pays the two drachmas
explanations.explanation: Close, but they don't ask about Peter. They ask Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, “Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas?” The question is about Jesus. Peter is just the one standing there to answer it.

explanations.answer: Whether the disciples pay the two drachmas
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd guess the whole group, since a tax question sounds like it could be for everybody. But the collectors come up to Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, and ask, “Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas?” I think that put Peter on the spot, because nobody likes getting asked about somebody else's bill. And he doesn't dodge it. He answers, “Yes.”
Peter answers, “Yes.” That's his response when the collectors ask if his Teacher pays the two drachmas. After that, Peter enters the house, and Jesus speaks to him first.
The text says the opposite. When the collectors ask whether his Teacher pays, Peter answers, “Yes.” Then Peter enters the house, where Jesus speaks to him first.

Peter answers, “From others.” Jesus had asked whether the kings of the earth collect customs and taxes from their own sons or from others. Peter picks the second one. Then Jesus says, “Then the sons are exempt…”
That's one of the two choices Jesus gives, but it isn't what Peter says. Peter answers, “From others.” Jesus replies, “Then the sons are exempt…” The sons are the ones who don't pay.
Jesus gives Peter two choices: their own sons or others. Peter doesn't say no one. He answers, “From others.” That leads straight into Jesus saying, “Then the sons are exempt…”

Jesus says the opposite. After Peter answers, “From others,” Jesus tells him, “Then the sons are exempt…” Exempt means they don't have to pay. Then He gives a plan so the collectors won't be offended.

That's right, friend. After Peter says, “From others,” Jesus tells him, “Then the sons are exempt…” So the sons don't pay. Jesus still sends Peter to the sea, though, and He says so that they may not offend them.

Jesus tells Peter that when he opens the mouth of the first fish he catches, he will find “…a four-drachma coin.” Then Jesus says, “Take it and give it to them for My tax and yours.” A coin is exactly what Jesus names.
Jesus doesn't mention a pearl. He says Peter will find “…a four-drachma coin.” in the fish's mouth. That's the thing he's told to take and give to the collectors. No jewelry in this one, friend.

Jesus doesn't say anything about a gold ring. He says Peter will find “…a four-drachma coin.” in the mouth of the first fish he catches. I'd have loved a ring, but I'll take the coin. It's the one Jesus says to give to the collectors.

Jesus covers more than just His own. He tells Peter, “Take it and give it to them for My tax and yours.” So the coin is meant for both of them. Peter's tax is included too, and Jesus says he'll find the coin in a fish's mouth.
That's right. Jesus tells Peter, “Take it and give it to them for My tax and yours.” The coin covers Jesus' tax and Peter's. It's one coin for the two of them.
